docs.title: How Each Lab Is Built
docs.text:
Every investigation follows the same structure as a SOC ticket:

  1. Trigger and scope: what fired or what I set out to find, the host, and the user.
  2. Evidence: raw Sysmon logs, PCAPs, or mail headers, with the queries used to pull them. Raw files live in the repo's evidence/ folder.
  3. Timeline and pivots: what happened, in order, backed by artifacts.
  4. Verdict: true or false positive, severity, and escalation call.
  5. Detection: a rule that catches it next time, tested against real lab data where I had it, and labeled clearly where I did not.

docs.title: Suspicious LSASS Memory Access (Splunk SPL)
docs.text:
Filters on Sysmon Event ID 10 where the target is lsass.exe and the access mask includes memory read permissions (0x1fffff, 0x1010, 0x1410), excluding core system processes.

index=botsv1 "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='SourceImage'>(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='TargetImage'>(?<TargetImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='GrantedAccess'>(?<GrantedAccess>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Computer>(?<host_name>[^<]+)</Computer>"
| where match(TargetImage, "(?i)\\\\lsass\.exe$")
| where match(GrantedAccess, "(?i)^0x(1fffff|1010|1410|1438|143a|1f3fff)$")
| where NOT match(SourceImage, "(?i)^C:\\\\Windows\\\\System32\\\\(svchost|wininit|csrss|services|lsm)\.exe$")
| eval severity=if(match(SourceImage, "(?i)\\\\(AppData|Temp|Users\\\\Public)\\\\"), "critical", "high")
| stats count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(GrantedAccess) as access by host_name SourceImage severity
| sort - count
View Sigma Rule Definition 
title: Suspicious Process Access to LSASS Memory
status: experimental
author: Mian Talha Nayyar
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1003.001
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_access
detection:
  selection:
    TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    GrantedAccess:
      - '0x1fffff'
      - '0x1010'
      - '0x1410'
      - '0x1438'
      - '0x143a'
      - '0x1f3fff'
  filter_system:
    SourceImage:
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\wininit.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\csrss.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\services.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\lsm.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_system
falsepositives:
  - EDR and antivirus monitoring agents
  - Legitimate administrator memory dumps via Task Manager
level: high

docs.title: Office Application Spawning Command Shell (Splunk SPL)
docs.text:
Detects living-off-the-land techniques where Microsoft Office applications spawn command interpreters (cmd.exe, powershell.exe) indicative of macro exploitation.

index=wineventlog EventCode=4688
| eval parent=lower(Creator_Process_Name), child=lower(New_Process_Name)
| where match(parent, "\\\\(winword|excel|powerpnt|outlook|onenote)\.exe$")
    AND match(child, "\\\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32)\.exe$")
| table _time host Account_Name parent child Process_Command_Line

docs.title: Outbound Cleartext HTTP from Internal Workstation (Splunk SPL)
docs.text:
Isolates direct outbound cleartext HTTP (port 80) connections originating from endpoints using non-standard or scripted user agents.

index=proxy dest_port=80
| where NOT match(http_user_agent, "(?i)(mozilla|windows-update|microsoft)")
| stats count values(url) as urls dc(dest) as destinations by src http_user_agent
| where count > 5

docs.title: Failed Logons Followed by Success (KQL)
docs.text:
Correlates 10 or more failed network or RDP logons (wrong password or nonexistent user) with a successful logon from the same source to the same host within 10 minutes. Full write-up, test results, and tuning notes in Lab 05.

let lookback = 1h;
let failureThreshold = 10;
let successWindow = 10m;
let failures = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where EventID == 4625
    | where LogonType in (3, 10)
    | where SubStatus in~ ("0xc000006a", "0xc0000064")
    | where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress !in ("-", "127.0.0.1", "::1")
    | summarize
        FailureCount = count(),
        FirstFailure = min(TimeGenerated),
        LastFailure = max(TimeGenerated),
        AccountsTried = make_set(TargetUserName, 50)
        by IpAddress, Computer
    | where FailureCount >= failureThreshold;
let successes = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where EventID == 4624
    | where LogonType in (3, 10)
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, IpAddress, Computer, SuccessAccount = TargetUserName;
failures
| join kind=inner successes on IpAddress, Computer
| where SuccessTime between (FirstFailure .. (LastFailure + successWindow))
| project FirstFailure, LastFailure, SuccessTime, AttackerIP = IpAddress, VictimHost = Computer,
    SuccessAccount, FailureCount, AccountsTried
| order by SuccessTime desc

docs.title: Password Spraying from One Source (KQL)
docs.text:
Many accounts, few attempts each, from one source IP in a 15-minute window.

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4625 and LogonType in (3, 10)
| where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress !in ("-", "127.0.0.1", "::1")
| summarize Attempts = count(), DistinctAccounts = dcount(TargetUserName),
    Accounts = make_set(TargetUserName, 25) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where DistinctAccounts >= 5 and Attempts <= DistinctAccounts * 3

docs.title: Windows and Sysmon Event ID Reference
docs.text: The events I rely on most in investigations, and what each one tells me.

docs.title: Windows Security Log: Logons and Accounts
docs.text: Event ID What it records What I look for 4624 Successful logon Logon type, source IP, and whether it follows a run of failures 4625 Failed logon SubStatus (why it failed), source IP, volume over time 4634 / 4647 Logoff Session length when building a timeline 4648 Logon with explicit credentials runas or a tool using alternate credentials, often lateral movement 4672 Special privileges assigned at logon An admin-level logon; unusual for that user is a red flag 4720 User account created New accounts outside the normal provisioning process 4724 Password reset attempt Reset by someone other than the user or helpdesk 4728 / 4732 / 4756 Member added to a global / local / universal security group Anyone added to Domain Admins or local Administrators 4740 Account locked out Brute force against one account, and the source machine name 1102 Security log cleared Almost always worth an immediate look

docs.title: Windows Security Log: Execution and Persistence
docs.text: Event ID What it records What I look for 4688 New process created Parent-child lineage and the command line, if enabled 4697 Service installed (Security log) Services running from user-writable paths 4698 Scheduled task created Tasks that run scripts or binaries from Temp or AppData 7045 Service installed (System log) Same as 4697; present even when 4697 auditing is off 4104 PowerShell script block logged (PowerShell Operational log) The decoded script content, even if it was obfuscated

docs.title: Domain Controller: Kerberos and NTLM
docs.text: Event ID What it records What I look for 4768 Kerberos TGT requested Requests for accounts without pre-authentication (AS-REP roasting) 4769 Kerberos service ticket requested Many requests with RC4 encryption (0x17) from one user: Kerberoasting 4771 Kerberos pre-authentication failed Failure code 0x18 is a bad password; high volume is guessing or spraying 4776 NTLM credential validation Failures across many accounts from one workstation

docs.title: Logon Types (4624 / 4625)
docs.text: Type Name Typical source 2 Interactive At the keyboard or console 3 Network SMB file shares, most remote tooling, also brute force over SMB 4 Batch Scheduled tasks 5 Service A service starting under an account 7 Unlock Workstation unlock 8 NetworkCleartext Credentials sent in cleartext, for example basic authentication 9 NewCredentials runas /netonly; also used by some credential theft tools 10 RemoteInteractive RDP 11 CachedInteractive Logon with cached domain credentials, off network

docs.title: 4625 Failure Codes (SubStatus)
docs.text: Code Meaning What it suggests 0xC000006A Wrong password for a real account Password guessing 0xC0000064 Account does not exist Username enumeration or spraying guessed names 0xC0000072 Account disabled Attempts on dormant accounts 0xC0000234 Account locked out Lockout triggered 0xC0000071 Password expired Often a stale service account, not an attack 0xC0000193 Account expired Contractor or temporary account still in use somewhere 0xC000006F Logon outside allowed hours Policy violation or stolen credentials used off hours 0xC0000070 Logon from an unauthorized workstation Credentials used from the wrong machine

docs.title: Sysmon
docs.text: Event ID What it records What I look for 1 Process creation, with hashes and parent command line The richer version of 4688 3 Network connection Processes that should not talk to the internet, like rundll32 or Office 7 Image (DLL) loaded Unsigned DLLs loaded into trusted processes 8 CreateRemoteThread Code injection into another process 10 Process access Anything opening lsass.exe with memory-read rights (0x1010, 0x1410, 0x1fffff). See Lab 03 11 File created Dump files, dropped executables, files in startup folders 12 / 13 / 14 Registry key and value changes Run keys and other persistence locations 22 DNS query The process behind a suspicious domain lookup 23 File deleted (archived) Attackers cleaning up after themselves

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Every technical term used in this portfolio, explained in plain English.

docs.title: Core Security Operations
docs.text: Term Plain-English meaning SOC (Security Operations Center) The team that monitors a company's systems for attacks and responds to them Alert An automatic warning raised when activity matches a pattern that might be an attack Triage Quickly deciding whether an alert is real and how urgent it is True positive An alert that correctly caught real malicious activity False positive An alert that fired on something harmless. Too many of these bury the real attacks Benign true positive The alert was technically correct, but the activity was authorized, like an admin doing approved maintenance Incident A confirmed security event that needs a response Escalation Handing a serious case to a more senior team, usually incident response Containment Stopping an attack from spreading: disabling an account, isolating a computer, blocking an address Playbook A step-by-step guide for responding to a specific type of incident Threat hunting Searching for attackers proactively, before any alert fires Detection / detection rule A saved search that runs automatically and raises an alert when it finds a match Detection engineering Writing, testing, and tuning those rules Tuning Adjusting a rule so it stops firing on harmless activity without missing real attacks MTTD / MTTR Mean time to detect and mean time to respond: how fast the team notices and stops an attack

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Term Plain-English meaning SIEM A central system that collects logs from everywhere and lets analysts search them. Splunk and Microsoft Sentinel are SIEMs Splunk A widely used SIEM. Its search language is SPL Microsoft Sentinel Microsoft's cloud SIEM. Its search language is KQL Azure Data Explorer A Microsoft data service that also uses KQL; I used its free tier to test queries EDR Software on each computer that watches program behavior and can isolate the machine. CrowdStrike Falcon is an EDR SOAR Automation that performs routine response steps without an analyst doing them by hand Sysmon A free Microsoft tool that records detailed activity on Windows: programs starting, network connections, file changes Wireshark A tool for opening and reading recordings of network traffic CyberChef A web tool for decoding and transforming data, often used on suspicious email content Sigma A shared format for writing detection rules once and converting them to any SIEM Regex (regular expression) A pattern for finding and pulling specific text out of messy data

docs.title: Windows and Logs
docs.text: Term Plain-English meaning Log A timestamped record of something that happened on a computer Event ID The number Windows assigns to each type of log entry. 4625 means "failed logon," for example. See the Event ID Reference Process A running program Parent / child process The program that started another program, and the program it started. Word starting PowerShell is a classic warning sign Baseline What normal looks like, so abnormal stands out Logon type How someone logged in: at the keyboard, over the network, or by remote desktop Domain controller The server that manages every account and login in a company network. Compromise it and you control the company Active Directory Microsoft's system for managing users, computers, and permissions across a company LSASS The Windows process that holds logged-in users' passwords and login tickets in memory. Attackers try to copy it to steal credentials Memory dump A copy of a program's memory saved to a file. A dump of LSASS contains passwords LOLBin (living off the land binary) A legitimate Windows tool abused by attackers, so their activity blends in. rundll32 and regasm are examples

docs.title: Attacks
docs.text: Term Plain-English meaning Credential dumping Stealing stored passwords or login tickets from a computer Brute force Guessing passwords over and over until one works Password spraying Trying one or two common passwords across many accounts, to avoid locking any single account out Phishing Fake emails pretending to come from a trusted source, to steal passwords or install malware Spoofing Faking the sender of an email so it looks legitimate Typosquatting Using a name that looks almost right, like "Netllx" instead of "Netflix" Tracking pixel An invisible image in an email that tells the sender when you opened it Macro Code embedded in an Office document. Attackers use it to run malware when "Enable Content" is clicked Lateral movement An attacker spreading from one compromised computer to others C2 (command and control) The channel an attacker uses to send instructions to a compromised computer Masquerading Disguising a malicious tool, for example by renaming it

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Term Plain-English meaning IOC (indicator of compromise) A clue that an attack happened: a malicious IP address, domain, file hash, or file name Defanging Rewriting a dangerous link so it cannot be clicked by accident, like hxxp://bad[.]com Hash (MD5, SHA256) A unique fingerprint of a file. If the hash matches a known malware sample, the file is that malware Packet / PCAP A packet is one small piece of network traffic. A PCAP file is a recording of many packets HTTP vs HTTPS Web traffic. HTTP is readable by anyone watching the network; HTTPS is encrypted User-Agent A label a program sends to websites saying what it is, like "Chrome on Windows" SPF / DKIM / DMARC Email authentication checks that verify a message really came from the domain it claims Timeline The attack events put in order, minute by minute MITRE ATT&CK A public catalog of attacker techniques, each with an ID like T1110 (Brute Force). The industry's shared vocabulary. See my coverage map Correlation Linking separate events together, like many failed logins followed by a success from the same address

docs.title: How I Triage an Alert
docs.text: The method I use when an alert lands in the queue, from first look to close or escalate.

docs.title: 1. The First Five Questions
docs.text:
Before touching a query, I answer these from the alert itself:

  1. What fired, and what is it designed to catch? Read the rule logic, not just the title.
  2. Who and what is involved? User, host, source and destination IPs, process.
  3. Is this normal for them? Has this user, host, or process done this before? Check a 7 to 30 day baseline.
  4. What happened right before and right after? Pull a time window of 15 minutes either side on the same host and user.
  5. If this is real, what is the impact? A domain controller or a finance user changes the urgency.

docs.title: 2. Verdicts
docs.text:
Verdict Meaning Example True positive Malicious activity the rule was built to catch procdump -ma lsass.exe from a Temp folder Benign true positive The rule worked correctly, but the activity is authorized IT admin creates an LSASS dump during a sanctioned troubleshooting ticket False positive The rule fired on activity it should not match An EDR agent's normal LSASS access matching a too-broad rule

A false positive is a rule problem: I tune it. A benign true positive is a context problem: I document it and consider an allowlist with an owner and an expiry date.

docs.title: 3. Severity
docs.text:
Low impact (single workstation, standard user) High impact (server, DC, privileged account, sensitive data) High confidence Medium Critical Low confidence Low High

Severity goes up immediately for any of: a successful logon after a brute force, credential access tools, activity on a domain controller, or signs of data leaving the network.

docs.title: 4. When I Escalate
docs.text:
I escalate to incident response when any of these are true:

  • Confirmed credential theft or a guessed password that worked
  • Malicious code ran, not just arrived
  • The same indicator appears on more than one host
  • A privileged account or domain controller is involved
  • I cannot rule out malicious activity within the triage time limit

INC-LAB03: LSASS memory dumped on two domain controllers

Verdict: True positive | Severity: Critical | Status: Escalated to IR

Summary: Multiple tools opened lsass.exe with full access (0x1fffff) and wrote memory dumps to disk on win-dc-807 and win-dc-262. Mimikatz then parsed a dump offline. Domain credentials should be treated as compromised.

Timeline (UTC, win-dc-807, 2020-11-03):

  • 15:52:58: Temp binary dropped by wce.exe, run as a SYSTEM service, opens LSASS 38 times
  • 15:52:59: procdump -ma lsass.exe writes lsass_dump.dmp
  • 15:53:03: rundll32 comsvcs.dll MiniDump and Outflank-Dumpert.exe write dumps
  • 15:53:03: mimikatz sekurlsa::minidump parses a dump

Detection coverage: live LSASS access is caught by the Lab 03 rule. Offline Mimikatz parsing is not, because it only shows up in process creation logs. Recommend a command line rule for sekurlsa.

docs.title: What a SOC Analyst Does
docs.text: This page explains my job in plain English, for anyone reading this portfolio, technical or not.

docs.title: The Short Version
docs.text:
A Security Operations Center (SOC) is the team that watches over a company's computers, networks, and accounts around the clock, looking for signs of an attack.

Think of a large office building. It has cameras in every hallway, badge readers on every door, and alarms on the windows. Someone has to sit in the security room, watch those feeds, and decide which alarms are real. A SOC analyst is that person for the company's digital building.

Every day, security tools generate alerts: "someone failed to log in 40 times," "a program tried to read passwords from memory," "an employee clicked a link in a suspicious email." Most alerts turn out to be harmless. My job is to quickly and correctly separate the real attacks from the noise, stop the real ones before they cause damage, and make the alarms smarter so they cry wolf less often.

docs.title: How an Alert Becomes a Decision
docs.text:
1. DetectA tool raises an alert 2. TriageIs it real? How serious? 3. InvestigateWhat happened, to whom, and how? 4. RespondContain, remove, recover, report 5. ImproveTune the rule, close the gap
  1. Detect. A security tool spots something matching a known pattern of attack and raises an alert.
  2. Triage. I decide quickly whether it is real and how urgent it is. Many alerts are closed here as harmless, with a written reason.
  3. Investigate. For anything that might be real, I pull the logs, follow the trail, and reconstruct exactly what happened, in order.
  4. Respond. If it is an attack, I contain it: disable the stolen account, isolate the infected computer, block the attacker's address. Serious cases are escalated to the incident response team.
  5. Improve. Every alert teaches something. If the alarm was wrong, I fix the rule. If an attack slipped through, I write a new rule so it gets caught next time.

My method for steps 2 to 4 is written out in How I Triage an Alert.

docs.title: Lab 01: Windows Process Creation Auditing (Event ID 4688)
docs.text:
Category: Endpoint Telemetry and Baselining ATT&CK: T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter | T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File Tools: Local Security Policy, Windows Event Viewer Host: Windows 10/11 lab workstation (DESKTOP-2UVTUII)

Verdict: Benign | Baseline established

The process captured (services.exe launching svchost.exe as SYSTEM) is normal Windows service startup. The value of this lab is the baseline and the detection logic it produced.

In plain English

What this is: Windows can keep a diary of every program that starts on a computer, but it is switched off by default. I switched it on and learned to read it.

Why it matters: Almost every attack involves running a program. If a Word document secretly opens a command window, this diary is how an analyst sees it. Without it, the SOC is blind on that computer.

What I did: Turned on process logging, generated activity, traced which program started which (the "parent" and "child"), and wrote a rule that flags Office apps launching command shells, a classic sign of a malicious document.

Result: The activity I captured was normal Windows startup, which gave me a baseline of what normal looks like. The detection rule is written and ready to test against a real attack.

Skills this lab shows: Windows audit policy Event ID 4688 Process lineage Baselining Splunk SPL

Key terms in this lab
  • Process: a running program
  • Parent / child process: the program that started another, and the one it started
  • Event ID 4688: the Windows log entry for "a new program started"
  • Baseline: what normal looks like, so abnormal stands out

Every term is explained in the Glossary.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Attackers lean on built-in Windows binaries to run commands, enumerate the host, and launch payloads. Windows does not log process creation by default, so without it a SOC is blind to most of that activity.

The goal: turn on process creation auditing, generate telemetry, and learn to read Event ID 4688 for parent-child process lineage.

docs.title: 2. Configuration
docs.text:
1. Opened secpol.msc and went to Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > System Audit Policies > Detailed Tracking.
  2. Enabled Audit Process Creation for Success and Failure.
  3. Filtered the Security log in Event Viewer to Event ID 4688.

Gap found: command lines are off by default

4688 only records the binary name unless you also enable Administrative Templates > System > Audit Process Creation > Include command line in process creation events. Without it you can see powershell.exe ran, but not the encoded payload it ran. This is the first setting I'd check in any new environment.

docs.title: A single 4688 event
docs.text: Field Value Meaning Event ID 4688 A new process was created Creator account SYSTEM (DESKTOP-2UVTUII$) Launched by the OS itself New process C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe The child Creator process C:\Windows\System32\services.exe The parent Mandatory label System Mandatory Level Highest integrity

docs.title: 4. Analysis
docs.text:
Process lineage is the core of endpoint triage. The question is never just "what ran" but "what launched it".

Parent Child Read services.exe svchost.exe Normal. This is how Windows starts services explorer.exe chrome.exe Normal. User opened a browser winword.exe powershell.exe Malicious until proven otherwise. Classic macro execution excel.exe cmd.exe Malicious until proven otherwise. Same pattern wmiprvse.exe powershell.exe Suspicious. Common in remote WMI execution

docs.title: 5. Detection Logic
docs.text:
Office applications should almost never start a shell. This SPL flags it from Windows Security logs:

index=wineventlog EventCode=4688
| eval parent=lower(Creator_Process_Name), child=lower(New_Process_Name)
| where match(parent, "\\\\(winword|excel|powerpnt|outlook|onenote)\.exe$")
    AND match(child, "\\\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32)\.exe$")
| table _time host Account_Name parent child Process_Command_Line

Status

Logic only. Next step is to trigger it with an Atomic Red Team macro test and record the results here.

docs.title: 6. Takeaways
docs.text:
• Know the baseline first. svchost.exe is normal. svchost.exe launched by anything other than services.exe is not.
  • Enable command line logging. Process names without arguments leave the most important evidence out.
  • Sysmon Event ID 1 is the upgrade. It adds hashes, parent command lines, and process GUIDs, which is what Lab 03 relies on.

docs.title: Lab 02: Network Traffic Analysis and HTTP Stream Reconstruction
docs.text:
Category: Network Forensics ATT&CK: T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols | TA0011 Command and Control Tools: Wireshark (Protocol Hierarchy, Endpoints, Follow TCP Stream) Evidence: http.cap (public Wireshark sample capture)

Verdict: Benign in this capture | Pattern worth alerting on

The session is a terminal browser pulling a public directory listing. Nothing malicious was downloaded, but cleartext HTTP from a non-standard client is exactly what C2 and scripted downloads look like on the wire.

In plain English

What this is: A network recording (a PCAP) is like a transcript of every conversation computers had over the network. I replayed one conversation between a computer and a web server.

Why it matters: When a hacked computer contacts its attacker, the network recording often shows it, even if the attacker wiped the logs on the computer itself.

What I did: Filtered the recording down to just the web requests, rebuilt the full back-and-forth conversation, and identified the unusual program that made the request.

Result: This traffic was harmless: a text-only web browser downloading a public file list. I documented the pattern worth alerting on, which is unencrypted web traffic from programs that are not normal browsers.

Skills this lab shows: Wireshark Packet analysis HTTP IPv6 Client fingerprinting

Key terms in this lab
  • PCAP: a recording of network traffic
  • HTTP vs HTTPS: unencrypted vs encrypted web traffic
  • User-Agent: the label a program uses to identify itself to a website
  • C2: the channel an attacker uses to control a hacked computer

Every term is explained in the Glossary.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text: When endpoint logs are missing or wiped, packets are still the source of truth. The goal: triage a capture, isolate application-layer requests, rebuild the full session, and pull out the artifacts an analyst would put in a ticket.

docs.title: 2. Method
docs.text:
1. Scoped the capture. Used Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy for the protocol mix and Statistics > Endpoints (IPv6) for who talked to whom.
  2. Filtered to requests. Applied http.request to drop transport noise and keep only client-initiated web requests.
  3. Rebuilt the session. Used Follow > TCP Stream to read the request and response as one conversation.

Useful filters for this kind of triage:

http.request                              # client requests only
http.request and !(http.user_agent contains "Mozilla")   # non-browser clients
http.response.code >= 400                 # errors and blocked requests
tcp.port == 80 and ip.src == <internal>   # cleartext traffic leaving a host

docs.title: Reconstructed TCP stream
docs.text: Artifact Value Frame 49 Client 2001:6f8:102d:0:2d0:9ff:fee3:e8de (source port 59201) Server 2001:6f8:900:7c0::2 port 80 Host header cl-1985.ham-01.de.sixxs.net User-Agent Lynx/2.8.6rel.2 libwww-FM/2.14 SSL-MM/1.4.1 OpenSSL/0.9.8b Response HTTP/1.1 200 OK from Apache, open directory listing

docs.title: 4. Analysis
docs.text:
• Everything is readable. Over port 80 with no TLS, the headers, client identity, and full response are exposed. Any credentials sent here would be too.
  • The client is not a normal browser. Lynx is a terminal browser. On a corporate workstation, a non-standard User-Agent usually means a script, a tool, or something running without a user at the keyboard.
  • Open directory listing. The server exposed .pdf and .htm files. In a real case I'd carve anything downloaded with File > Export Objects > HTTP, hash it, and check the hash against threat intel.

docs.title: 5. Detection Logic
docs.text:
Cleartext outbound HTTP from workstations with an unusual User-Agent, using proxy or Zeek-style HTTP logs:

index=proxy dest_port=80
| where NOT match(http_user_agent, "(?i)(mozilla|windows-update|microsoft)")
| stats count values(url) as urls dc(dest) as destinations by src http_user_agent
| where count > 5

Status

Logic only. Next step is to run it against a capture with real beaconing (planned for Lab 07).

docs.title: 6. Takeaways
docs.text:
• Port 80 leaving a workstation is worth a look. Almost all legitimate web traffic is TLS now.
  • User-Agent is cheap context. It's not proof, since attackers can fake it, but an odd one is a fast way to prioritize.
  • Follow the stream. Single packets are fragments. The stream is what goes in the report.

docs.title: Lab 03: Threat Hunting LSASS Credential Dumping in Splunk
docs.text:
Category: SIEM Threat Hunting and Detection Engineering ATT&CK: T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory | TA0006 Credential Access Tools: Splunk Enterprise, SPL, Sysmon (Event IDs 1, 10, 11) Evidence: windows-sysmon.log (7,974 events) | Detection: detections/

Verdict: True Positive | Critical | Escalate to IR

Two domain controllers had LSASS memory dumped with six different methods, including a renamed binary built to evade name-based detection. Domain credentials should be treated as compromised.

In plain English

What this is: After breaking into one computer, attackers try to steal passwords from its memory so they can spread to others. I searched through nearly 8,000 security log entries from two attacked servers to find out exactly how they did it.

Why it matters: These were domain controllers, the servers that control every login in a company. Stolen passwords there are effectively the keys to the whole building.

What I did: Narrowed 851 events down to 55 suspicious ones, separated normal Windows activity from six different attack methods, rebuilt the attack minute by minute, and wrote a detection rule that catches the behavior even when the attacker renames their tools.

Result: The rule flagged every tool that read the password store, and raised zero false alarms on the 108 normal events. That makes it a strong starting point for a production rule, pending tuning on a real environment's baseline.

Skills this lab shows: Splunk SPL Regex field extraction Sysmon Threat hunting Timeline reconstruction Detection engineering Sigma

Key terms in this lab
  • LSASS: the Windows process that holds logged-in users' passwords in memory
  • Credential dumping: copying those stored passwords out of memory
  • Domain controller: the server that manages every account in a company
  • False positive: an alarm on something harmless

Every term is explained in the Glossary.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
lsass.exe holds credentials, Kerberos tickets, and NTLM hashes in memory. Dumping it is how attackers move from one compromised host to the whole domain.

The goal: ingest raw Sysmon telemetry into Splunk, separate attack activity from normal system noise, rebuild the attack timeline, and ship a detection that does not depend on tool names.

docs.title: 2. Data Source
docs.text:
Field Value Telemetry Sysmon Operational log, raw XML Key events 10 ProcessAccess, 1 ProcessCreate, 11 FileCreate Hosts win-dc-807.attackrange.local, win-dc-262.attackrange.local Event time range 2020-11-03 to 2021-02-03 (UTC) Adversary simulation Atomic Red Team T1003.001, run in Splunk Attack Range

Index name

I loaded the log into a local Splunk index named botsv1. The data itself is Attack Range telemetry, not the BOTS v1 dataset.

docs.title: Step 1: Broad sweep
docs.text:
Every event mentioning LSASS, as source or target:

index=botsv1 "lsass.exe"

Result: 851 events. Too broad to triage, since LSASS also appears as the source of normal activity.

docs.title: Step 2: Extract fields from raw XML
docs.text:
The log was ingested as raw XML with no field parsing, so I extracted SourceImage with rex and narrowed to Event ID 10:

index=botsv1 "lsass.exe" "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='SourceImage'>(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| stats count by SourceImage

Result: 750 events from 14 source processes. Atomic Red Team binaries stand out immediately, but this view still mixes in normal Windows processes.

docs.title: Step 3: Isolate who opened LSASS, and with what rights
docs.text:
Event ID 10 records the access mask (GrantedAccess). Reading LSASS memory requires PROCESS_VM_READ (0x0010), so masks like 0x1fffff (full access) and 0x1410 are what dumping looks like. Routine system access is usually 0x1400 or 0x1000.

index=botsv1 "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='SourceImage'>(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='TargetImage'>(?<TargetImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='GrantedAccess'>(?<GrantedAccess>[^<]+)</Data>"
| where match(TargetImage, "(?i)\\\\lsass\.exe$")
| stats count by SourceImage GrantedAccess
| sort - count

Result: 163 processes opened LSASS directly. 108 were normal Windows processes with low access masks. 55 were not.

Stage Events What changed Keyword sweep 851 Any event mentioning lsass.exe Event ID 10 only 750 Process access events, LSASS as source or target LSASS as target 163 Something opened LSASS Benign baseline 108 svchost, wininit, csrss, services with low access masks Alerts 55 Non-system processes with memory-read access

docs.title: Step 4: Pivot to process creation and file events
docs.text:
Event ID 10 shows who touched LSASS but not the command line. To confirm intent I pivoted to Event ID 1 (process creation) and Event ID 11 (file creation), looking for the command lines and the dump files they wrote.

index=botsv1 ("<EventID>1</EventID>" OR "<EventID>11</EventID>")
  ("lsass" OR "comsvcs" OR "mimikatz" OR ".dmp")
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='CommandLine'>(?<CommandLine>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='TargetFilename'>(?<TargetFilename>[^<]+)</Data>"
| table _raw CommandLine TargetFilename

docs.text: Source Process Access Count Host Assessment AppData\Local\Temp\644c305e-...d1d.exe 0x1fffff 38 dc-807 Malicious. Dropped by wce.exe (Windows Credentials Editor) and run as a SYSTEM service by services.exe procdump.exe / procdump64.exe 0x1fffff 6 both Malicious. procdump -ma lsass.exe wrote lsass_dump.dmp notprocdump.exe / notprocdump64.exe 0x1fffff 3 dc-262 Malicious. Renamed ProcDump to evade name-based rules Outflank-Dumpert.exe 0x1fffff 2 dc-807 Malicious. Direct syscall dumper, wrote dumpert.dmp rundll32.exe 0x1fffff, 0x1410 2 dc-807 Malicious. comsvcs.dll MiniDump, a living-off-the-land dump taskmgr.exe 0x1fffff, 0x1410 3 dc-262 Suspicious. Interactive admin session created lsass (2).DMP from Task Manager powershell.exe 0x1410 1 dc-807 Needs context. Occurred 1 second after LSASS started at boot, before the attack chain

docs.title: Dump files written to disk (Event ID 11)
docs.text: Time (UTC) Host Writer File 2020-11-03 15:52:59 dc-807 procdump64.exe C:\Windows\Temp\lsass_dump.dmp 2020-11-03 15:53:03 dc-807 rundll32.exe ...\AppData\Local\Temp\lsass-comsvcs.dmp 2020-11-03 15:53:03 dc-807 Outflank-Dumpert.exe C:\Windows\Temp\dumpert.dmp 2021-02-03 16:51:01 dc-262 procdump64.exe C:\Windows\Temp\lsass_dump.dmp 2021-02-03 16:51:14 dc-262 notprocdump64.exe C:\Windows\Temp\lsass_dump.dmp 2021-02-03 21:34:57 dc-262 taskmgr.exe ...\AppData\Local\Temp\2\lsass (2).DMP

docs.title: Attack timeline: win-dc-807, 2020-11-03 (UTC)
docs.text:
Time Activity 15:52:48 PowerShell checks that dumping tools exist on disk (Test-Path ...\procdump.exe, mimikatz.exe) 15:52:58 wce.exe drops a GUID-named binary to Temp, which runs as a SYSTEM service and opens LSASS 38 times 15:52:59 procdump -accepteula -ma lsass.exe writes a full memory dump 15:53:03 rundll32 comsvcs.dll MiniDump and Outflank-Dumpert.exe each write a dump 15:53:03 mimikatz.exe "sekurlsa::minidump %tmp%\lsass.DMP" "sekurlsa::logonpasswords full" parses a dump offline 15:53:06 Cleanup: del lsass_dump.dmp, del dumpert.dmp, Remove-Item lsass-comsvcs.dmp

Key observation: Mimikatz never touched live LSASS. It parsed a dump file offline, so it does not appear in Event ID 10 at all. Only process creation logging (Event ID 1) caught it. A detection built only on Event ID 10 would miss this step.

docs.title: Indicators
docs.text: Type Value SHA256 7234C8F98B87593641BBDB594E34C94B9436986C4FB70E7DA5BCECFF147D14C3 (Temp service binary) MD5 605560CA0624AABF9F53675257B9BE21 File path C:\Users\ADMINI~1\AppData\Local\Temp\644c305e-30f4-470b-b616-d924c3206d1d.exe Tool directory C:\AtomicRedTeam\atomics\T1003.001\bin\ Dump files lsass_dump.dmp, lsass-comsvcs.dmp, dumpert.dmp, lsass (2).DMP Account ATTACKRANGE\Administrator

docs.title: 5. Detection Rule
docs.text:
Built to catch the behavior, not the tool name: any non-system process opening LSASS with memory-read rights.

index=botsv1 "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='SourceImage'>(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='TargetImage'>(?<TargetImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='GrantedAccess'>(?<GrantedAccess>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Computer>(?<host_name>[^<]+)</Computer>"
| where match(TargetImage, "(?i)\\\\lsass\.exe$")
| where match(GrantedAccess, "(?i)^0x(1fffff|1010|1410|1438|143a|1f3fff)$")
| where NOT match(SourceImage, "(?i)^C:\\\\Windows\\\\System32\\\\(svchost|wininit|csrss|services|lsm)\.exe$")
| eval severity=if(match(SourceImage, "(?i)\\\\(AppData|Temp|Users\\\\Public)\\\\"), "critical", "high")
| stats count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(GrantedAccess) as access by host_name SourceImage severity
| sort - count

docs.title: Validation against the lab data
docs.text:
Metric Result LSASS access events evaluated 163 Alerts fired 55 Alerts tied to confirmed dumping 54 Alerts needing analyst context 1 (PowerShell at boot) Benign system accesses alerted 0 of 108 Renamed notprocdump.exe caught Yes, matched on behavior, not name

A Sigma version is in the detection library for porting to other SIEMs.

docs.title: 6. Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Detect the access mask, not the filename. notprocdump.exe would slip past a rule looking for "procdump". It cannot hide its 0x1fffff request to LSASS.
  2. Event ID 10 alone is not enough. Offline parsing with Mimikatz only shows up in process creation logs. Pair access monitoring with command line monitoring for sekurlsa, MiniDump, and -ma lsass.
  3. Watch for dump files. An Event ID 11 rule for *.dmp files containing "lsass" is a cheap second layer that caught every dump here, including the Task Manager one.
  4. Check your timestamps. Splunk set _time to my ingest time because the raw XML was not timestamp-parsed. The real event times came from the SystemTime field. In production, configure TIME_PREFIX in props.conf so timelines are correct.

docs.title: 7. Response Actions
docs.text:
• Isolate win-dc-807 and win-dc-262 from the network.
  • Reset passwords for every account with an active session on both hosts, starting with ATTACKRANGE\Administrator.
  • Reset the krbtgt account twice to invalidate forged Kerberos tickets.
  • Hunt for the SHA256 above and for *.dmp files across all endpoints.
  • Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) and Credential Guard on domain controllers.

docs.title: Lab 04: Inbound Phishing Analysis and Header Forensics
docs.text:
Category: Phishing Triage ATT&CK: T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment | T1566.002 Spearphishing Link | TA0001 Initial Access Tools: Raw header analysis (RFC 5322), CyberChef, URL defanging, static document review Samples: TryHackMe Phishing Analysis module (training samples, analysis and write-up are my own)

Verdict: All samples malicious | Block, purge, and hunt for clicks

Every sample impersonated a known brand and either harvested credentials or delivered a payload. None should reach a user inbox.

In plain English

What this is: Phishing emails pretend to come from trusted brands to trick people into giving up passwords or opening malware. I analyzed real phishing samples from a training set.

Why it matters: Most breaches start with an email. Catching a phishing campaign early, and finding everyone who clicked, is one of the most common things a SOC does.

What I did: Compared who each email claimed to be from with where it really came from, followed the links through their redirects, examined the attachments, and built a list of indicators to block.

Result: Every sample was malicious. The response plan: remove them from every inbox, block the senders and links, and check whether anyone clicked.

Skills this lab shows: Email header analysis SPF / DKIM / DMARC URL and redirect analysis IOC extraction Response planning

Key terms in this lab
  • Spoofing: faking the sender of an email
  • Email header: the hidden routing details that show where an email really came from
  • IOC: a clue such as a bad domain or file name, used for blocking
  • Defanging: rewriting a link so it cannot be clicked by accident

Every term is explained in the Glossary.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Phishing is still the most common way attackers get in. Modern lures use brand impersonation, lookalike names, and multi-stage redirects to get past email gateways.

The goal: triage reported emails the way a SOC queue would, check headers for sender spoofing, trace links and redirects, review attachments, and produce a clean IOC set for blocking.

docs.title: 2. Triage Summary
docs.text: Sample Lure Technique Verdict Action PayPal receipt Fake transaction Display name spoofing, foreign envelope sender Malicious Block sender domain, purge Netflix suspension Account on hold Typosquatted display name, PDF with a payment link to a non-Netflix domain Malicious Block sender, purge, check for clicks Shared-file lure Document waiting URL shortener, tracking pixel, multi-hop redirect to fake Outlook login Malicious Block domains, reset any user who clicked Apple billing Blank body, attachment only .dot template that pulls remote macros Malicious Block attachment type, hash hunt DHL delivery "Enable content" spreadsheet .xlsx lure designed to launch regasm.exe Malicious Block, hunt for regasm.exe from Office

docs.title: Phase 1: Headers and sender identity
docs.text:
The display name and the real sending address did not match in either brand-impersonation sample:

  • PayPal: Displayed service@paypal.com, but the envelope sender came from sultanbogor[.]com, a domain with no relationship to PayPal.
  • Netflix: Display name Netllx billing, with "fi" swapped for "ll" so it reads as Netflix at a glance. Sent from z99@musacombi[.]online. The body pushed an attached PDF whose "Update Payment Account" link pointed to a non-Netflix domain, padded with a real Netflix help link and an odd-format phone number to look legitimate.

Mail clients show the display name prominently and hide the routing path. That gap is what these lures depend on.

What I check in every header:

Header Why it matters From vs Return-Path A mismatch is the fastest spoofing signal Authentication-Results SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass or fail for the claimed domain Received chain (read bottom up) The true origin server and any odd relays Reply-To Often points to an attacker inbox even when From looks clean

docs.title: Phase 2: Links, tracking pixels, and redirects
docs.text:
1. URL shortener. Links went through hxxps://is[.]gd/6oCJ4m to hide the real landing page from scanners.
  2. Tracking pixel. A 1x1 image (tracking.png on devret[.]xyz) told the attacker the mailbox was live and the email was opened.
  3. Redirect chain. Links bounced through lookalike file-sharing pages (Citrix → OneDrive → Adobe) before landing on a fake Microsoft Outlook login page built to harvest credentials.

docs.title: Phase 3: Attachments
docs.text:
When links get blocked, attackers switch to attachments:

  • Apple .dot template. Blank email body, just the attachment. Word templates can fetch macros from a remote server when opened, so the file looks clean until it runs.
  • DHL .xlsx. The spreadsheet told the user to click "Enable Content", the step that lets embedded code run and launch regasm.exe, a signed Windows binary attackers abuse to run payloads.

docs.title: 4. IOCs (defanged)
docs.text: Type Indicator Context Sender domain sultanbogor[.]com PayPal impersonation Sender address z99@musacombi[.]online Netflix impersonation Tracking domain hxxp://devret[.]xyz Tracking pixel host Short link hxxps://is[.]gd/6oCJ4m Hides credential harvesting page Attachment Apple_Receipt.dot Remote template macro loader Process regasm.exe launched by Excel Living-off-the-land execution

docs.title: 5. Response and Detection
docs.text:
Immediate response

  • Purge every sample from all mailboxes, not just the reporter's.
  • Block the sender domains, tracking domain, and short link at the gateway and proxy.
  • Search proxy logs for anyone who reached the short link or the fake Outlook page. Any hit means a password reset and session revoke for that user.

Hardening

  1. Enforce DMARC alignment. Quarantine or reject mail where the From domain fails SPF alignment or has no valid DKIM signature.
  2. Block risky attachment types from external senders: .dot, .dotm, .xltm, and macro-enabled Office files.
  3. Automate triage. Have SOAR parse reported .eml files, defang links, expand shorteners in a sandbox, and check every domain against threat intel.

Endpoint detection for the DHL sample

index=sysmon EventCode=1
| where match(ParentImage, "(?i)\\\\(excel|winword)\.exe$")
    AND match(Image, "(?i)\\\\regasm\.exe$")
| table _time host User ParentImage Image CommandLine

docs.title: Lab 05: Brute Force Detection Logic in KQL
docs.text:
Category: Identity Detection Engineering ATT&CK: T1110.001 Password Guessing | T1110.003 Password Spraying | T1033 System Owner/User Discovery Query language: KQL, written for the Microsoft Sentinel SecurityEvent table Test environments: Azure Data Explorer (simulated data), my Windows workstation (real 4625 events)

Simulated scenario: read this first

The attack story below (host FIN-WKSTN-04, account CORP\jdoe, source 192.168.10.45) is a scenario I designed to build and test detection logic. It is not a real incident and no containment took place. The KQL was tested in Azure Data Explorer against a small hand-built dataset, and separately against real failed logons I generated on my own machine. Running it against live Sentinel telemetry is planned as Lab 05 v2.

In plain English

What this is: Brute force means guessing a password over and over until one works. I wrote search logic that spots many failed logins followed by a successful one from the same place.

Why it matters: One wrong password is normal. Dozens of failures in minutes, then a success, means someone probably guessed their way in.

What I did: Designed an attack scenario, tested the search logic on sample data, then tested it against real failed logins on my own computer. That real test exposed two blind spots, which I fixed.

Result: An improved rule, plus a second rule for password spraying. The next step is running both on a real cloud SIEM with live data.

Skills this lab shows: KQL Windows logon events Correlation logic Detection testing Tuning

Key terms in this lab
  • Brute force: guessing one account's password repeatedly
  • Password spraying: trying a few common passwords across many accounts
  • KQL: the search language for Microsoft Sentinel
  • Event IDs 4625 / 4624: Windows log entries for a failed and a successful login

Every term is explained in the Glossary.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
A single failed logon means nothing. Users mistype passwords all day. What matters is many failures followed by a success from the same source, because that means the attacker probably got in.

The goal: write KQL that correlates repeated Event ID 4625 failures with a 4624 success, test the logic, and find out where it breaks.

docs.title: 2. How Windows Records Logons
docs.text:
Event ID Meaning Why it matters here 4625 An account failed to log on Source IP, target account, logon type, and the failure reason 4624 An account logged on successfully Tells you whether the guessing worked 4688 A new process was created Shows what the attacker did next, if process auditing is on

The SubStatus field on 4625 tells you why the logon failed, and that changes what you are looking at:

SubStatus Meaning What it suggests 0xC000006A Account exists, wrong password Password guessing against a real account 0xC0000064 Account does not exist Username enumeration, or spraying a list of guessed names 0xC0000072 Account disabled Attempts against dormant accounts 0xC0000234 Account locked out Lockout policy triggered, often by brute force

Note

0xC000006D usually appears in the Status field ("unknown user name or bad password"). The SubStatus carries the specific reason. Always read SubStatus.

Logon types matter too: 3 is network (SMB, for example), 10 is RDP, 2 is interactive at the keyboard. See the Event ID Reference for the full list.

docs.title: 3. Scenario Design (simulated)
docs.text:
The scenario I built the rule around:

Time (UTC) Event Detail Meaning 14:02:11 4625 CORP\jdoe, from 192.168.10.45, Logon Type 3, SubStatus 0xC000006A Guessing starts 14:14:05 4625 142nd failure in 12 minutes Too fast and too regular for a human 14:14:28 4624 CORP\jdoe, from 192.168.10.45, Logon Type 3 The password was guessed 14:15:10 4688 whoami /all run on FIN-WKSTN-04 under CORP\jdoe Attacker checks who they are and what groups they have (T1033)

docs.title: 4. Test 1: Correlation Logic in Azure Data Explorer
docs.text:
I don't have live Sentinel data for this scenario, so I tested the join logic in Azure Data Explorer's free query environment. I wrote the two event summaries as a datatable and ran the correlation against them.

let failedLogons = datatable(FirstFailure:datetime, LastFailure:datetime, TargetAccount:string, Computer:string, IpAddress:string, FailureCount:int)
[
    datetime(2026-10-14 14:02:11), datetime(2026-10-14 14:14:05), "CORP\\jdoe", "FIN-WKSTN-04", "192.168.10.45", 142
];
let successfulLogons = datatable(SuccessTime:datetime, TargetAccount:string, Computer:string, IpAddress:string, LogonType:int)
[
    datetime(2026-10-14 14:14:28), "CORP\\jdoe", "FIN-WKSTN-04", "192.168.10.45", 3
];
failedLogons
| join kind=inner (successfulLogons) on TargetAccount, Computer, IpAddress
| project FirstFailure, LastFailure, SuccessTime, TargetAccount, Computer, SourceIP = IpAddress, FailureCount, LogonType

The join returns one row matching the failures to the success on account, host, and source IP. This proves the join keys and output columns work. It does not prove the thresholds or field formats against real Sentinel data.

What this test proves: the join keys line up and the output is what an analyst needs. What it does not prove: how the rule behaves on real, messy telemetry. That is what Test 2 is for.

docs.title: 5. Test 2: Real Failed Logons on My Workstation
docs.text:
Next I generated real failed network logons on my own machine (DESKTOP-2UVTUII) against the account name jdoe, which does not exist there, and looked at what Windows actually recorded.

Real Event ID 4625 from my workstation: Logon Type 3, Status 0xC000006D, SubStatus 0xC0000064 (user does not exist), source network address 127.0.0.1.

This real event exposed two gaps in my first version of the rule:

What the real event showed Problem with version 1 Fix in version 2 SubStatus 0xC0000064, not 0xC000006A v1 only matched wrong-password failures, so attacks against nonexistent accounts (enumeration, spraying guessed names) were invisible Match both SubStatus values Source 127.0.0.1 v1 excludes loopback, so this local test could never fire Correct for production, since loopback failures come from local services. For local testing, remove that filter temporarily

Also, version 1 grouped by target account. That catches one account being hammered but misses password spraying, where an attacker tries one password across many accounts. Version 2 groups by source IP and host instead and records which accounts were tried.

docs.title: 6. Detection Rule v2 (Sentinel SecurityEvent)
docs.text:
let lookback = 1h;
let failureThreshold = 10;
let successWindow = 10m;
let failures = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where EventID == 4625
    | where LogonType in (3, 10)
    | where SubStatus in~ ("0xc000006a", "0xc0000064")
    | where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress !in ("-", "127.0.0.1", "::1")
    | summarize
        FailureCount = count(),
        FirstFailure = min(TimeGenerated),
        LastFailure = max(TimeGenerated),
        AccountsTried = make_set(TargetUserName, 50)
        by IpAddress, Computer
    | where FailureCount >= failureThreshold;
let successes = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where EventID == 4624
    | where LogonType in (3, 10)
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, IpAddress, Computer, SuccessAccount = TargetUserName;
failures
| join kind=inner successes on IpAddress, Computer
| where SuccessTime between (FirstFailure .. (LastFailure + successWindow))
| project FirstFailure, LastFailure, SuccessTime, AttackerIP = IpAddress, VictimHost = Computer,
    SuccessAccount, FailureCount, AccountsTried
| order by SuccessTime desc

docs.title: Companion rule: password spraying
docs.text:
Spraying looks different: many accounts, few attempts each, to stay under lockout thresholds.

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4625 and LogonType in (3, 10)
| where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress !in ("-", "127.0.0.1", "::1")
| summarize Attempts = count(), DistinctAccounts = dcount(TargetUserName),
    Accounts = make_set(TargetUserName, 25) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where DistinctAccounts >= 5 and Attempts <= DistinctAccounts * 3

Validation status

Both rules are written for the Sentinel SecurityEvent schema. They have not yet been run against live Sentinel data. Thresholds (10 failures, 5 accounts) are starting points that would need tuning against a real baseline.

docs.title: 7. Expected False Positives and Tuning
docs.text: Source of noise Why it fires How to handle it Service account with an expired password Retries every few seconds, forever Find and fix the service; allowlist only after fixing User who just changed their password Phone or mapped drive keeps using the old one Usually low count, single account; check the device Vulnerability scanners Authenticated scans try many logons Allowlist scanner IPs, but alert if they ever succeed unexpectedly VPN or NAT gateways Many users share one source IP Group by account as well, or exclude the gateway and use VPN logs

docs.title: 8. If This Fired for Real: Response Steps
docs.text:
1. Confirm: check the 4624 for the logon type, the time gap from the last failure, and whether the source IP is normal for this user.
  2. Scope: look for other successes from the same IP, and any 4688 process activity under the account after the logon.
  3. Contain: disable the account or force a password reset, kill active sessions, and isolate the source host if it is internal.
  4. Escalate: a confirmed guessed password is a true positive at High severity. Escalate to IR with the timeline.
  5. Prevent: enforce MFA, review lockout policy, and block legacy NTLM where possible.

docs.title: 9. Takeaways
docs.text:
• Test against real events, not just your assumptions. One real 4625 from my own machine found two gaps the simulated test never would have.
  • SubStatus changes the story. 0xC000006A means a real account is being guessed. 0xC0000064 means someone is guessing names.
  • Group by source to catch spraying. Grouping by account only catches one account being hammered.
  • Next: Lab 05 v2 runs these rules against real telemetry from a Windows VM sending logs to a Sentinel workspace.
